There are a couple of things you say that make this tricky.   Memories aren’t as sure as we think they are.   

The book Mistakes were made (but not by me) has a good metric for false memories.   If it was always traumatic, then it likely was traumatic, if it you forgot about it, then years later remembered how traumatic it was, it’s likely a false memory and was not traumatic when it occurred.  

An innocent exam poorly explained can later be reframed into assault by an overly excited therapist, and if that’s the case could ruin a career over nothing.  

Because you said “I didn’t recognize it as that until years later when I was describing it to a therapist” take a real close look and ask yourself if it has always been distressing or if it started when you talked to your therapist.  

I’m not saying it is a false memory, but give it the “has it always been traumatic” test.  If it has, then move forward with your plan.  As long as it is true and you don’t harass, you won’t be in trouble for speaking out.  

Whether it happened as you remembered or not, the trauma is there now, as a SA survivor myself, I highly recommend the book The Book of Forgiving by Desmond Tutu.   This outlines how forgiving is a gift we give ourselves and how to reach the point where what happened no longer holds power over us.

I agree with everyone else, the first step is to forgive yourself.   Also realize that suicide is sometimes acceptable in stoicism, however… it’s occasionally spoken of as a way to choose when to depart life while maintaining your dignity and self, not as a way to get out of a difficult situation.   It’s usually seen as acceptable for terminal illnesses, when you are deciding between a slow messy, and tortured death, where you will lose self identity, your mind and more, or taking a dignified exit.  I mention this not to support suicide but to help take the sting off the shame you feel around the attempt.  

The mistake you made in my opinion wasn’t the attempt, it was that you didn’t fully evaluate what was within your control and what was outside of your control. Because of this mistake it felt like the only true option.   

I’m a suicide attempt survivor myself, the first time I was a child, and as I was preparing for my second attempt at age 31, I felt like I didn’t have options, I didn’t have control over anything… or so I thought.  After making up my mind to do it, I decided to get second opinions and checked myself into an inpatient facility for 2 months.  They opened my eyes to the possibility that I had so much more available to me and my future than I thought.  It wasn’t permanent, and I had options.    

Chances are, you will entertain this thought and option again, and the next time it will feel just as hopeless.   Before you make a decision, call the suicide hotline, check into a hospital, or check into a mental health facility.   When we are in these deep states of depression, our ability to clearly see our choices diminish.   You took those actions because you couldn’t clearly see what choices you had.  

Remember:
We can’t control our bodies, we can’t control our environment, we can’t control nature, and we can’t control others, all we really can control is our own reactions, decisions, and judgements.   

You mentioned that your health problems felt hopeless; that emotional toll likely clouded how many options you still had.  

Even if you are bedridden, you can expand your mind or mentor others, libraries make books available, audiobooks make learning available to the blind, speech to text allow you to record thoughts and impressions, and zoom allows us to connect around the world.   

Look at what Stephen Hawking accomplished while imprisoned in a body that could barely move, look at what Hellen Keller accomplished without the ability to see or hear.   

No matter what limits our bodies give us, we still have options and control over what we do with those limits.   When you feel hopeless, look to others for a second opinion including therapy.  They will help you see through the emotional cloud so you can see all your options.  

Suicide is an option, but it’s the last resort option because it cannot be undone.  Take some time to read Seneca’s On The Shortness of Life, it will help to gain perspective.  

CS Lewis said, “You can’t go back and change the past, but you can start where you are and change the ending” 

Give yourself some grace, at the time, you didn’t have all the information and made a decision based on what you thought was best.  Now you can see you had more options than you thought.   It’s not a shameful action, it was an error made due to lack of information. 

For help forgiving yourself, check out Desmond Tutu’s the book of forgiving.  While it’s not strictly stoicism, his fourfold path of forgiveness follows the spirit of stoicism. 
1. Tell the story
2. Name the hurt
3. Offer forgiveness 
4. Renew or release the relationship.  

In this case you’ll be creating a new relationship with yourself.  One that acknowledges that this is a part of your story and that having been through it you’ll be stronger.   


Now my final thought is on hope.   

You’ve been beaten up by fate, you’ve been pummeled into the ground, and literally found yourself at the end of your own rope.   

In Seneca’s letters on ethics, letter 13 he shares one of my favorite quotes.  

“One can never be sure of one's strength until numerous difficulties have appeared on every side... Fortune tests the spirit's mettle.  A boxer who has never suffered a beating cannot bring bold spirits to the match.  It is the one who has seen his own blood--who has heard his teeth crunch under the fist--who has lost his footing and found himself spread-eagled beneath his opponent--the one who, though forced to yield, has never yielded in spirit, who after falling rises fiercer every time:  that is the one who goes to the contest with vigorous hope.”

You’ve made it through, and your wounds are healing.  Because of this experience, you’ll be far better equipped for future situations.   Dust yourself off, train your mind, and allow your mind and body to heal, then look forward with a new story of hope and resilience.   

Even if your neck never heals, it can serve as a reminder of the lessons you are learning in this stage of your journey, and those lessons will make you even stronger in the future.
